A hands-on learning adventure · beginner to builder JavaScript From Zero to Hero A deep, friendly guide to thinking in code, making websites interactive, and understanding how JavaScript can also work outside the browser. No experience needed—just curiosity. 19 bite-sized lessons Examples from first steps to advanced No libraries needed Made for ages 12+ Your mission: Don’t memorize every word. Read a little, type the examples yourself, change them, break them, and fix them. That is how programmers learn. Ask a trusted adult before installing software or running code from strangers. 01 Think like a coder Programming is giving a computer clear instructions to solve a problem. A computer is very fast, but it does exactly what its instructions say—not what you meant. Coding is the art of turning a big idea into tiny, unambiguous steps. 🧩 1. Understand What should happen? What information do you have? What result do you want? 🪜 2. Break it down Split the job into smaller steps. A recipe is an algorithm: a list of steps in order. 🛠️ 3. Write and test Tell JavaScript the steps. Try normal, tiny, huge, and surprising inputs. 🔎 4. Improve Read what happened, fix one thing at a time, and make the code easier to understand. Algorithm before code: packing a school bag Look at tomorrow’s timetable. For each class, add its books and supplies. If it is sports day, add sports clothes. Check the list, then close the bag. Notice the words for each and if ? They become loops and decisions in code. Before typing, explain your solution in ordinary words or draw a flowchart. Vocabulary: An algorithm is a repeatable set of steps. A bug is a problem in a program. Debugging means finding and fixing that problem. Bugs are normal—even experts make them. 02 Your first JavaScript JavaScript (often shortened to JS) is a programming language that makes things happen. Try the browser console: in most desktop browsers, open Developer Tools and choose Console . Type a line and press Enter. On a phone or tablet, use an online coding environment with a trusted adult. The console is a scratchpad; it is not the same as a text message box. console.log("Hello, world!"); console.log(2 + 3); console.log() prints a value so you can inspect it. Text goes inside quotes; numbers do not. The semicolon marks the end of a statement. JavaScript often allows you to leave it out, but using it consistently can make code easier to scan. JavaScript is not Java Despite their similar names, Java and JavaScript are different languages, like a car and a carpet are different even though both start with “car”. This guide teaches JavaScript. Try it: Change the greeting to your name. Then print the answer to 12 * 4 . Predict the result before pressing Enter. 03 Values and variables Values are the information your program works with. Variables give useful names to information. Three useful ways to create a variable const learner = "Mina"; // This name should keep pointing to this value let score = 0; // This value can be updated score = score + 10; console.log(learner, score); Kind Use it when… Example const You won’t assign a different value to this variable. const homePlanet = "Earth"; let You need to assign a new value later. let lives = 3; lives = 2; var Mostly in older code; learn to recognize it, but usually prefer const or let . var oldStyle = true; A variable is like a labeled box, but const means the label cannot be pointed at a different value. If a const contains an object or array, the contents may still be changed; we will see why in Lesson 09. Common value types const username = "Kai"; // string: text const age = 12; // number: includes whole and decimal numbers const isReady = true; // boolean: true or false const score = null; // intentionally no value let nextMove; // undefined: no value assigned yet const huge = 12345678901234567890n; // bigint: very large whole number JavaScript also has symbol , used for special unique identifiers. You usually won’t need it at first. Check a value’s type with typeof —but be aware of one old JavaScript surprise: typeof null says "object" . console.log(typeof "hello"); // "string" console.log(typeof 42); // "number" console.log(typeof true); // "boolean" Text and templates const hero = "Nova"; const level = 4; const message = `${hero} reached level ${level}!`; console.log(message); Backticks create a template literal . The ${...} parts insert JavaScript values into the text. Changing values and naming let coins = 5; coins = coins + 2; // now 7 coins += 3; // now 10 coins++; // now 11 Use names that explain what a value means: minutesLeft is clearer than x . JavaScript names are case-sensitive: score and Score are different. 04 Math and comparisons Computers are great at arithmetic, counting, and checking rules. Operator Meaning Example result + Add, or join strings 7 + 2 → 9 - Subtract 7 - 2 → 5 * Multiply 7 * 2 → 14 / Divide 7 / 2 → 3.5 % Remainder after division 7 % 2 → 1 ** Power 3 ** 2 → 9 Order matters: multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. Use parentheses to make your meaning obvious: (2 + 3) * 4 . Equality and comparisons console.log(5 > 3); // true console.log(5 === 5); // true: same value and type console.log(5 === "5"); // false: number is not text console.log(5 !== 4); // true: not equal Prefer === and !== for equality. The older == can convert types in surprising ways, so beginners should avoid it until they understand coercion. Comparisons include < , > , <= , >= . Logic: combine yes/no answers const hasTicket = true; const isOldEnough = true; console.log(hasTicket && isOldEnough); // AND: both must be true console.log(hasTicket || isOldEnough); // OR: either can be true console.log(!hasTicket); // NOT: flips true/false Think of logic like rules for a game. && means “and”, || means “or”, and ! means “not”. JavaScript’s && and || can return one of their original values, not just true or false ; that shortcut is useful later. Averages and rounding const points = [8, 10, 6]; const total = points[0] + points[1] + points[2]; const average = total / points.length; console.log(Math.round(average)); // 8 Computers use floating-point numbers, so some decimal calculations are tiny bit inexact (for example, 0.1 + 0.2 ). For money, store cents as whole numbers where possible: 199 cents is $1.99. 05 Make decisions Programs choose different actions with conditions. const temperature = 18; if (temperature >= 25) { console.log("Warm day!"); } else if (temperature >= 15) { console.log("A light jacket might help."); } else { console.log("Bundle up!"); } JavaScript checks conditions from top to bottom and runs the first matching branch. Curly braces { } hold the instructions in a block. Indentation is not required by the computer, but it helps people see the structure. Switch for a list of exact choices const day = "Saturday"; switch (day) { case "Saturday": case "Sunday": console.log("Weekend!"); break; default: console.log("School day"); } break stops the switch from continuing into the next case. For many simple choices, if / else is easier to read. Truthy and falsy (a later-level idea) Conditions can use values other than booleans. Values such as 0 , "" , null , undefined , and NaN act like false in a condition; most other values act like true. When learning, explicit checks can be clearer. const nickname = ""; if (nickname) { console.log(`Hi, ${nickname}!`); } else { console.log("No nickname yet."); } 06 Repeat with loops Loops save you from writing the same instruction over and over. Count with a for loop for (let round = 1; round Read it as: start at 1; keep going while the condition is true; add 1 after each turn. The three parts are separated by semicolons. Watch the condition carefully: a mistake can cause an endless loop. Repeat while something is true let energy = 3; while (energy > 0) { console.log("Play!"); energy--; } A while loop checks before each turn. Make sure each turn can eventually make its condition false. Otherwise it may never stop. Loop through a collection const snacks = ["apple", "toast", "yogurt"]; for (const snack of snacks) { console.log(`Pack: ${snack}`); } for...of is a friendly way to visit each item in an array or other iterable. Use break to stop early or continue to skip to the next turn. Loop safety: If a page freezes, a loop might be running forever. Stop the page or close its tab. In your own code, double-check the starting value, stopping condition, and update. 07 Functions: reusable recipes A function groups instructions under a name. Give it inputs; it can return an output. function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}!`; } const greeting = greet("Sam"); console.log(greeting); name is a parameter —a named input. "Sam" is an argument —the actual value we pass in. return sends a result back. A function can also do a task without returning a useful value. Function expressions and arrow functions const double = function (number) { return number * 2; }; const triple = (number) => { return number * 3; }; const quadruple = number => number * 4; console.log(double(5), triple(5), quadruple(5)); Arrow functions are a shorter way to write many functions. If the arrow function has one expression, parentheses and braces can be shortened; that expression is returned automatically. Use braces plus return when the steps need more room. Default inputs and input checking function welcome(name = "friend") { return `Welcome, ${name}!`; } function add(a, b) { if (typeof a !== "number" || typeof b !== "number") { return "Please give me two numbers."; } return a + b; } console.log(welcome()); console.log(add(4, 6)); Keep each function focused: one clear job, a helpful name, and predictable inputs and outputs. This makes it easier to test and reuse. 08 Arrays: lists of things Use an array when you have an ordered list of values. const colors = ["teal", "gold", "violet"]; console.log(colors[0]); // "teal"; the first position is 0 console.log(colors.length); // 3 colors.push("coral"); // add to the end colors.pop(); // remove the last item Array positions are called indexes and start at zero. The last valid index is array.length - 1 . A const array can still have items added or removed: the variable still points at the same array. Useful array tools const numbers = [2, 4, 6, 8]; const doubled = numbers.map(number => number * 2); const bigOnes = numbers.filter(number => number >= 6); const found = numbers.find(number => number === 4); const total = numbers.reduce((sum, number) => sum + number, 0); console.log(doubled, bigOnes, found, total); Tool What it does Changes original? map Make a new array by changing each item No filter Make a new array with items that pass a test No find Get the first item that passes a test No reduce Combine items into one answer, such as a total No sort Reorder items (by default, as text) Yes For numbers, sort with a comparison rule: numbers.slice().sort((a, b) => a - b) . slice() makes a copy first, so the original list stays in its old order. Arrays of arrays const seats = [ ["A1", "A2"], ["B1", "B2"] ]; console.log(seats[1][0]); // "B1" 09 Objects: describe a thing An object groups named pieces of information, called properties. const pet = { name: "Pixel", kind: "cat", age: 3, isHungry: false }; console.log(pet.name); // dot notation console.log(pet["kind"]); // bracket notation pet.isHungry = true; Objects are useful when values belong together. A property’s name is its key . Use dot notation when you know the key; use brackets when you have the key in a variable or the name has special characters. Methods: functions that belong to objects const player = { name: "Rin", score: 0, earn(points) { this.score += points; return `${this.name} now has ${this.score} points.`; } }; console.log(player.earn(10)); In this method, this refers to the object that called it. this behaves differently in some kinds of functions; when that feels confusing, use a named parameter or read about arrow-function this rules later. Destructuring and spread const { name, score } = player; // take properties into variables const upgradedPlayer = { ...player, level: 2 }; // copy + add const newColors = [...["blue", "green"], "gold"]; // copy + add Objects are shared by reference: Assigning const otherPet = pet does not make a separate pet. Both names point to the same object. Spreading with { ...pet } makes a shallow copy: nested objects still need more care. JSON: a text format for data const saved = JSON.stringify(pet); // object → JSON text const restored = JSON.parse(saved); // JSON text → object JSON looks similar to JavaScript objects but is stricter: keys and text must use double quotes, and JSON cannot contain functions or undefined . Only parse JSON you trust or handle parse errors. 10 Scope, errors, and debugging Scope is where a name can be used. Debugging is careful detective work. const outside = "I can be used below"; function showMessage() { const inside = "I only exist in this function"; console.log(outside, inside); } showMessage(); // console.log(inside); // Error: inside is out of scope let and const are block-scoped: they live inside the nearest pair of braces where they were declared. Prefer small scopes and avoid reusing the same name for different ideas. Three kinds of problems Syntax error: the code is not written in a way JavaScript understands (perhaps a missing quote or bracket). Runtime error: the code starts, but something goes wrong while it runs. Logic bug: it runs, but gives the wrong answer. A calm debugging checklist Read the whole error message and note the line number. Check spelling, quote marks, brackets, and capitalization. Print intermediate values with console.log() . Test the smallest example that shows the problem. Change one thing, run again, and see whether it helped. Ask: what did I expect, what happened, and what is the first place they differ? function average(a, b) { const total = a + b; console.log("Checking total:", total); // temporary detective clue return total / 2; } console.log(average(8, 10)); Browser Developer Tools offer a debugger. A breakpoint pauses the program on a chosen line so you can inspect variables one step at a time. 11 JavaScript on the web: the DOM HTML describes a page, CSS styles it, and JavaScript can respond and update it. HTML The page structure: headings, buttons, paragraphs, images. CSS The appearance: colors, layout, spacing, motion. JavaScript The behavior: reacting, calculating, updating, communicating. Módulo 0: A Origem de um Superpoder Antes de escrevermos código, precisamos entender o nosso universo. O JavaScript (JS) nasceu em 1995, criado por Brendan Eich na empresa Netscape. Surpreendentemente, ele foi criado em apenas 10 dias! Se a Web fosse uma pessoa: HTML é o esqueleto (a estrutura, ossos). CSS é a roupa e a maquilhagem (o visual, estilo). JavaScript é o cérebro, os músculos e o sistema nervoso (a inteligência, reações e dinamismo). O JavaScript corre diretamente no teu navegador (browser) sem precisar de instalar programas complexos. É a linguagem que faz os jogos web, botões interativos e animações funcionarem. Módulo 1: As Caixas Mágicas (Variáveis e Tipos de Dados) Para programar, precisamos de guardar informação na memória do computador. Fazemos isso usando variáveis . Pensa nelas como caixas onde colamos uma etiqueta com um nome. // Criamos uma caixa chamada 'nomeHeroi' e guardamos um texto (String) let nomeHeroi = "Alex"; // Criamos uma caixa constante (que não muda) chamada 'idade' com um número const idade = 12; // Uma variável lógica (Boolean) que diz se ele está ativo let estaAtivo = true; Tipos de Dados Fundamentais: String : Sequência de caracteres (texto), sempre entre aspas ( "Olá" ). Number : Números inteiros ou decimais ( 12 , 3.14 ). Boolean : Verdadeiro ( true ) ou Falso ( false ). Módulo 2: O Grimório Secreto (A Documentação Oficial) Nenhum herói memoriza todos os feitiços do mundo. Os programadores usam a documentação oficial, sendo a mais famosa a MDN Web Docs (Mozilla Developer Network) . Quando lês a documentação, encontras a sintaxe (como escrever) e os parâmetros (o que a função precisa para funcionar). Por exemplo, a documentação explica que a função console.log() serve para imprimir mensagens na consola do navegador para testes. Módulo 3: Tomando Decisões (Lógica e Condicionais) Um programa inteligente precisa de tomar decisões, tal como tu quando decides se levas guarda-chuva ou não com base no estado do tempo. let nivelPoder = 85; if (nivelPoder >= 90) { console.log("És um Herói de Elite!"); } else if (nivelPoder >= 50) { console.log("Estás no bom caminho, jovem aprendiz!"); } else { console.log("Precisas de treinar mais!"); } Módulo 4: Feitiços Reutilizáveis (Funções) As funções são pequenos blocos de código encapsulados que executam uma tarefa específica. Em vez de repetires o mesmo código várias vezes, crias uma função e chamas-a sempre que precisares. // Declaração da função function calcularDano(forcaAtaque, multiplicador) { let danoTotal = forcaAtaque * multiplicador; return danoTotal; // Devolve o resultado final } // Aplicação (Chamada da função) let golpeFinal = calcularDano(25, 3); // golpeFinal agora vale 75 Repara como os valores passados dentro dos parênteses ( 25 e 3 ) são os parâmetros que a função interpreta para realizar o cálculo matemático. Knowing their names is the easy part; knowing which one answers your question , which flags keep you inside scope, and which two tools only look alike is the job. This manual covers 63 tools across eight families — reconnaissance, web, credentials, wireless, exploitation, sniffing, Active Directory and forensics — with the command that does the work and the mistake that ends an engagement. 63 tool cards 8 families authorised targets only 1 file · no external assets Find a tool All Recon Web Passwords Wireless Exploit Sniff AD Forensics 63 tools · showing all sections 00 Before you touch a keyboard Authorisation, scope, evidence, stop conditions Kali does not make an action legal, and neither does an article. The difference between a penetration test and a crime is a signed scope, a test window and a person who can tell you to stop. Read this page before the tool pages; the commands assume you have already done it. The legal baseline Unauthorised access, interception and modification of systems or data are criminal offences in most jurisdictions, including Portugal (Lei do Cibercrime, Lei n.º 109/2009) and Brazil (Lei n.º 12.737/2012, the Lei Carolina Dieckmann ), and civilly actionable elsewhere. "I was only scanning" is not a defence when the scan was not authorised. This is not legal advice: your lawyer and your client define the contract. The blog has longer arguments about why this matters: Ethical Hacking , Pentesting Society and Interpretation of Attacks and Security Choices . If you have not read them, the short version is: capability is not permission , and the target's safety is part of the job. The six-line contract Parties. Who is authorised to test, on whose behalf, and who signs. Assets. Exact domains, IP ranges, cloud accounts, applications, APIs and accounts in scope — plus an explicit exclusion list. Time. Start, end, blackout periods, rate limits and whether out-of-hours work is allowed. Rules. No denial of service, no social engineering, no data exfiltration beyond proof, no persistence without consent. Stop. A named contact, an out-of-band channel, and the conditions that end the test immediately. Data. Where evidence lives, how it is encrypted, who can read it, when it is destroyed. That sentence explains both its strength and its main operational risk: you inherit Debian's package ecosystem and Kali's rolling pace, including fresh tools and fresh bugs. It is a workstation for assessments, not a hardened server and not an invisibility cloak. The Penetration Testing Execution Standard and the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide are the standard reference maps; this page is the tool-level companion. 03 Reconnaissance & OSINT Hosts, names, ports, services — and the difference between a lead and a fact Recon is where you earn the rest of the engagement. Passive collection uses public records and third-party sources; active collection sends packets to the target and can be logged, rate-limited or reported. Do passive first, write down every source, and never let a scanner's timeout become a conclusion. 14 cards passive → active scope first Your recon is also evidence about you DNS queries, certificate-transparency lookups, user agents and scan sources are visible to the target and to third parties. Use infrastructure you are authorised to use, not a borrowed VPS, and never assume Tor makes an active scan anonymous — it usually makes it slower and more suspicious. nmap pkg: nmap What it does. The reference port scanner: host discovery, TCP/UDP port states, service and version detection, OS guesses and the NSE scripting engine. It is the tool you use to understand a host, not merely to find an open port. copy sudo nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24 -oA evidence/scans/discovery sudo nmap -sS -p- --min-rate 1000 -oA evidence/scans/all-tcp 10.10.10.5 sudo nmap -sCV -p 22,80,443 --script safe -oA evidence/scans/services 10.10.10.5 Run it Broad discovery first, then all TCP ports, then a narrow service/script pass. Save with -oA ; a scan without output is a rumour. Use -Pn when ICMP is filtered, -T2 on fragile links, --reason to see why a port is marked open. Avoid -T5 on production or WAN links, --script vuln as a first move (noisy and occasionally disruptive), and UDP sweeps of entire ranges. Closed and filtered are different findings. Instead of masscan or rustscan for speed; nmap for truth. -sT works without raw sockets but is more connection-heavy; -sS is the usual choice when you have root. masscan pkg: masscan What it does. An asynchronous TCP port scanner with its own userland network stack. It trades accuracy and depth for raw speed across very large address ranges: no service detection, no scripts, no OS fingerprinting. copy sudo masscan -p1-65535 10.10.10.0/24 --rate=1000 \ --exclude 10.10.10.1 -oL evidence/scans/masscan.lst Run it Only on ranges you own or are authorised to test. Start at --rate 1000 , watch for packet loss, then verify every hit with nmap. Add --wait 3 so late replies are not lost. Avoid Internet-wide scans, rates that saturate a shared uplink, and treating a masscan miss as "closed". Its stack can be less reliable than the kernel's, especially behind NAT or stateful firewalls. Instead of Use it to find candidates across /16s and /8s; hand each live host to nmap. For a single host or a /24, rustscan is usually more convenient and nmap alone is already fast enough. rustscan pkg: rustscan What it does. Finds open TCP ports quickly, then automatically hands the open ports to nmap for service and script detection. Think of it as a fast front door with nmap waiting inside. copy rustscan -a 10.10.10.5 --ulimit 5000 -- -sV -sC -oA evidence/scans/rustscan Run it Everything after -- is passed to nmap. Raise --ulimit only on a machine you control. Use -b to tune batch size and --scan-order random to reduce obvious sequential patterns. Avoid Assuming its result is more accurate than nmap. It is a convenience wrapper; the nmap pass is what produces the evidence. Do not run high concurrency through a fragile VPN or IDS-heavy path. Instead of Use rustscan for a quick "which ports are open?" on one host; nmap directly when you need careful timing or complex NSE; masscan for enormous ranges. arp-scan pkg: arp-scan What it does. Discovers hosts on the local Layer-2 segment using ARP requests. Because ARP is not routed, it is authoritative only for the subnet you are plugged into — and it often finds devices that ignore ICMP. copy sudo arp-scan -I eth0 --localnet --retry 2 Run it Use --localnet or an explicit CIDR, and confirm the interface with ip -brief addr . Repeat once to catch sleeping devices. The vendor column comes from the MAC OUI and is a hint, not proof. Avoid Using it to infer hosts behind a router; ARP does not cross L3 boundaries. Do not confuse a silent host with an absent one — some stacks rate-limit ARP replies. Instead of nmap -sn is better for routed discovery; arp-scan is better for the local wire and for finding quiet appliances. Compare both before declaring a subnet empty. dnsrecon pkg: dnsrecon What it does. Enumerates DNS records and infrastructure: standard record types, zone-transfer attempts, SRV records, cache snooping and dictionary-based subdomain brute force. It is the quick, scriptable DNS check before a heavier mapping tool. copy dnsrecon -d example.com -t std --json evidence/recon/dnsrecon.json dnsrecon -d example.com -t brt \ -D /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt Run it Start with -t std , then targeted -t axfr against each authoritative name server. Brute force only with permission and a sensible wordlist; use --threads conservatively so you do not poison your own resolver. Avoid Treating NXDOMAIN as proof a name does not exist (wildcards and split-horizon DNS exist), and brute-forcing a third-party domain you merely found in a certificate. Instead of dnsenum adds scraping and whois; fierce is lighter and focuses on non-contiguous IP space; amass is the deep mapping tool. dnsrecon is the fast first pass. dnsenum pkg: dnsenum What it does. A Perl-era DNS enumeration script: record lookups, zone-transfer attempts, subdomain brute force, reverse lookups and optional search-engine scraping. It remains useful because its output is compact and its zone-transfer routine is blunt. copy dnsenum --enum example.com \ -f /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -r Run it Use --enum as the shortcut and -r for recursive brute force. Save the terminal output; dnsenum's file output is less structured than dnsrecon's JSON. Avoid Relying on its Google scraping — search providers block or change formats constantly. Do not run recursion without a time limit; it can expand quickly. Instead of Prefer dnsrecon for clean JSON and current record types, or amass for a serious map. Keep dnsenum for a quick second opinion or an environment where it is already installed. fierce pkg: fierce What it does. A focused DNS reconnaissance tool for finding hosts in non-contiguous IP space: it resolves names, tests zone transfers, detects wildcards and brute-forces subdomains with a small, fast workflow. copy fierce --domain example.com \ --subdomains /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt Run it Read the wildcard warning: if every random name resolves, brute-force results are meaningless until you filter the wildcard address. Keep the default timeouts for public DNS and raise them only in a lab. Avoid Using it as an attack tool — it is a resolver and a mapper. It will not find names that only exist in internal DNS, and it cannot see hosts that never appear in DNS. Instead of Faster to type than amass and cleaner than dnsenum for a single domain. Choose amass when you need certificates, ASNs, API sources and a graph; choose fierce for a five-minute answer. whois pkg: whois What it does. Queries the registration system for a domain, IP or ASN: registrar, creation and expiry dates, name servers, registrant organisation (when not redacted) and abuse contacts. RDAP is the modern JSON successor. copy whois example.com whois -h whois.iana.org example.com curl -s https://rdap.org/domain/example.com | jq '.events, .nameservers' Run it Query the authoritative registry for the TLD, then the registrar. Record the retrieval date; registration data goes stale. Use RDAP when you need machine-readable output. Avoid Trusting redacted fields or assuming the registrant is the operator. Privacy services, resellers and subsidiaries routinely hide the real owner. Do not use whois data for social engineering outside scope. Instead of DNS tells you what resolves now; whois tells you who registered it and when. They answer different questions and often disagree. theHarvester pkg: theharvester What it does. Collects public emails, hostnames, employee names and URLs from search engines, certificate transparency and other sources. It is contact-and-surface OSINT, not a port scanner. copy theHarvester -d example.com -b duckduckgo,bing,crtsh -l 300 \ -f evidence/recon/harvester Run it Use crtsh for certificate-history hostnames, and add API keys in /etc/theHarvester/api-keys.yaml for paid or rate-limited sources. Keep -l modest and save the HTML/JSON report. Avoid Assuming an email belongs to a current employee, or that a hostname still resolves. Verify before use. Respect provider terms and anti-spam law; harvested addresses are not a mailing list. Instead of amass maps infrastructure; theHarvester finds people and contact points; SpiderFoot automates both with correlation. Use the lightest one that answers the question. amass pkg: amass What it does. Maps an organisation's external attack surface: subdomains, IPs, ASNs, certificate names and relationships. Passive mode uses public sources; active mode adds DNS resolution, brute force and zone walking. copy amass enum -passive -d example.com -o evidence/recon/amass-passive.txt amass enum -active -d example.com -brute -w wordlist.txt \ -o evidence/recon/amass-active.txt Run it Passive first, always. Configure API keys in ~/.config/amass/config.yaml for better coverage, set -timeout , and keep the JSON output for the graph. Read the log: amass tells you which sources failed. Avoid Launching -active against a client's production DNS without warning — it is noisy. Do not assume the result is complete; private DNS, split horizon and CDNs hide whole estates. Instead of Use amass when scope is a whole organisation and you need relationships; dnsrecon/fierce for a quick domain check; theHarvester when the question is people, not infrastructure. recon-ng pkg: recon-ng What it does. A modular OSINT framework with workspaces, a database and import/export. You load modules, set a source

Military: Manual Técnico · Nível de Operações Infiltrar sem ser a força: leitura de estruturas grupais e de redes criminosas Uma orientação técnica para forças de segurança que pretendem agir com precisão, justiça e sem reproduzir os erros alheios ao próprio Estado. Ref. MT-2026-04 Idioma: pt-PT Acesso por nível (sequencial) Este manual foi concebido para leitores das forças armadas, polícias e serviços de inteligência. Não ensina a cometer crimes; ensina a não cometer crimes enquanto se protege a ordem . A leitura é sequencial: cada nível depende do anterior. Nível 1 Tráfico de confusão: polícia, militar, crimes e inocência Antes de agir, é preciso saber o que é e onde . Este nível diferencia tipos de organização, distingue o inocente do criminoso e explica porque razão a “solução militar” raramente é a resposta correta. 1.1 Tipos de organização que se confundem Muitas vezes, o problema não é a “organização criminosa” em si, mas a mistura de categorias . Conheça as seguintes famílias: Organizações criminosas (OC) – estruturas cuja finalidade é o lucro ilícito (tráfico, evasão fiscal, corrupção estruturada). Podem ter hierarquia, mas não são Estados nem forças armadas. Redes de apoio / comércio informal – redes que existem para partilha de recursos, proteção mútua ou subsistência, mas que podem ser instrumentalizadas por OC. Grupos de resistência política / civis armados – podem ser legítimos ou ilegítimos consoante o enquadramento legal do Estado. A distinção é jurídica, e não apenas moral. Forças de segurança do Estado – polícia, militares, serviços de inteligência. Têm mandato, formação e (em tese) responsabilidade perante a lei. Glossário rápido Inocente : não apresenta elementos objetivos de participação num crime. Criminoso : pessoa contra a qual existe prova (ou elementos de prova) suficiente para sustentar uma acusação. Suspeito : pessoa sobre a qual recaem indícios, mas sem padrão conclusivo. A distinção é técnica, não emocional. 1.2 Crime é crime — quem quer que o cometa Uma decisão errada é grave onde e quando for cometida . Se uma força de segurança atua com exagero, desrespeita inocentes ou recolhe provas de forma ilícita, a responsabilidade é da entidade que atua , e não de “ter mau comportamento porque o outro também é mau”. Exemplo de raciocínio incorreto (a evitar): Erro no raciocínio “Se a organização criminosa já recorreu à violência, a polícia também pode exagerar.” Isto é uma dupla medida : substitui a lei pela retaliação. A força de Estado perde legitimidade quando copia a desonestidade alheia. 1.3 Porque razão a diferenciação é uma técnica, e não uma opinião Diferenciar o inocente do criminoso exige padrões observáveis e prova , e não impressões. O raciocínio base utiliza: comportamento cognoscível (e não opiniões); traços de comunicação (canal, ritmo, linguagem, repetição); indicadores económicos (fluxo de recursos, armadilhas financeiras, contas falsas); relacionamentos documentados (quem está sempre no centro, quem é periférico); atuação narrativa (quem decide, quem apenas obedece). A: grupo legítimo / de apoio · B: organização criminosa · ⬤ centro operacional Grupo legítimo Organização criminosa Interface de contacto Dinâmica: estruturas fluidas, não estáticas 1.4 Sobre o que se sabe: fontes de informação legítimas Para conhecermos a atividade de uma OC sem nos tornarmos numa OC, recorremos a fontes e métodos que preservam a legalidade: observação pública e aberta (presença, padrões de movimento, fachada comercial falsa); inteligência de fontes abertas (OSINT): registos comerciais, comunicação pública, publicações, grupos de referência, anomalias nas comunicações; inteligência humana (HUMINT) através de fontes próprias, cuja identidade e segurança são devidamente protegidas; análise de comunicações com respeito pelo enquadramento legal e pelas limitações de intervenção livre; análise económica e financeira: rastreio de fluxos, titularidade de empresas, movimentos anómalos. Nível 1 concluído? Compreenda a diferença de abordagem no Nível 2 . Avançar → Nível 2 Nota: este manual tem carácter educativo e não substitui a instrução jurídica, operacional ou ética interna. As referências indicadas são materiais de apoio; em cada contexto, consulte o ordenamento jurídico aplicável. Nível 2 Ler a estrutura: como identificar atividade, influência e comando Mesmo sem atuar diretamente como militar ou polícia, é possível aprender a ler uma rede a partir de sinais , padrões e repetições . Este nível ensina a leitura técnica de redes e grupos. 2.1 As redes não são árvores Muitas organizações criminosas parecem hierárquicas, mas na prática funcionam como redes compostas por: nós centrais (poucos, com muita influência); nós periféricos (muitos, com pouca influência); pontes de contacto (nós que ligam dois subgrupos); rotas de comunicação (canal principal, canais de reserva); e lacunas (espaços onde a informação não passa — úteis para isolamento). 2.2 O que se observa Frequência de comunicação — quem aparece sempre, quem desaparece e reaparece, quem nunca aparece; Assinatura de canal — canal de comunicação preferido, padrão repetido, fuso horário/horário de atividade, marcas linguísticas (forma de expressão); Movimento de pessoas — quem se desloca constantemente, quem permanece fixo, quem apenas surge em condições específicas; Foco de decisão — a operação segue sempre a mesma pessoa ou coligação? Quem corrige, quem desvia. Nó central (centro de comando/influência) Nós ligados Nós periféricos Leitura: ligações mais sólidas = relações mais estáveis 2.3 Como desenvolver uma análise rigorosa recolher dados sem preconceitos — começar com padrões e não com suposições; notar anomalias relacionais, e não apenas “pessoas que parecem suspeitas”; fazer a distinção entre correlação e causalidade — “aparecerem juntos” não prova cumplicidade; “decidirem e agirem em conjunto” já pesa mais; cruzar fontes: se a comunicação aponta para um centro, mas a atividade económica aponta para outro, há uma camada a descobrir. Técnica de leitura “Quando o comandante não é visível, observe quem corrige o rumo quando a operação falha. O verdadeiro centro costuma revelar-se nos momentos de tensão, e não nos momentos de rotina.” 2.4 Inserção / acesso sem recurso à “força” Para entrar num grupo sem revelar a identidade de força de segurança, a estratégia base consiste na adoção de um papel : não surgir como um observador externo, mas sim como alguém com interesses convergentes (não necessariamente criminais — por exemplo, alguém com dúvidas ou alguém que “julga poder ajudar”); parâmetros de comunicação compatíveis (canal, linguagem, ritmo, paciência); evitar forçar a posição; a infiltração resulta melhor quando o grupo sente que o contacto é desinteressado ou útil. Grupo-alvo Observador / agente com papel próximo Aproximação sem revelar a origem — observação prévia ao envolvimento Nível 2 concluído? Vamos confrontar a teoria com exemplos reais no Nível 3. Avançar → Nível 3 Nível 3 Abordagens psicológicas e sociais: compreensão, influência e decisões corretas As competências que melhoram a análise não são estritamente técnicas — são também psicológicas e sociais . Este nível explora como a leitura de pessoas e grupos previne decisões erradas. 3.1 Leitura psicológica de grupos Os grupos (criminosos ou não) partilham dinâmicas semelhantes: Inércia grupal — o grupo tende a manter a direção uma vez estabelecida, mesmo quando o contexto muda; Liderança informal — nem sempre o líder é quem formalmente comanda; muitas vezes é quem corrige, quem medeia conflitos ou quem mantém a rede unida; A comunicação não-verbal é fundamental — o silêncio, o ritmo, quem fala menos e quem fala mais revelam frequentemente mais do que aquilo que é verbalizado; Vulnerabilidade social — os grupos são frágeis nas suas dependências estruturais: comunicação, recursos, confiança e acesso a pessoas-chave. 3.2 Influência sem coerção É possível influenciar um grupo sem recorrer à força, à detenção ou à violência direta: alterar as perceções de risco (sem recorrer a mentiras — através da disponibilidade de informação, do exemplo ou de alterações contextuais); alterar os incentivos (por exemplo, tornando mais oneroso o uso de uma determinada rede do que de outra); isolar lentamente os pontos centrais — não por destruição direta, mas através do desgaste de confiança; compreender que o grupo responde a normas internas — caso essas normas se tornem contraditórias, o grupo tende a desestabilizar-se. Atenção A influência não visa a manipulação para fins criminosos. Constitui um instrumento de análise: utilizar a perceção e a dinâmica para compreender o funcionamento do grupo e avaliar quando é possível desmantelá-lo sem derramamento de sangue ou detenções indevidas. 3.3 Quando não é necessário deter nem abater Muitas vezes, o problema reside em apenas uma parte da rede , e não na rede na sua totalidade. A decisão mais precisa é aquela que: visa diretamente a pessoa ou atividade verdadeiramente responsável; evita a punição genérica e indiscriminada; protege os inocentes que orbitam em redor do grupo; preserva a legitimidade da força de segurança. As detenções ou o recurso à força devem ser proporcionais e fundamentados em provas , e nunca motivados pela dimensão da rede, pela impaciência ou pelo espírito de vingança. 3.4 Riscos de uma análise incorreta tomar o comportamento por prova — o facto de alguém estar “sempre junto” não constitui prova de culpa; análise por perfil — discriminar com base na aparência, origem ou associação revela incompetência técnica e injustiça legal; viés de confirmação — partir do pressuposto de que “aquele grupo é totalmente corrupto” cega o investigador para identificar quem é inocente no seu interior. 3.5 Quem sabe o que sabe — e porque razão isso importa Para conhecer a atividade de um grupo, é necessário dispor de fontes externas ao grupo e observá-lo de dentro para fora . Isto implica: observar o que é público, mas sabendo ler nas entrelinhas; ouvir o que a própria comunidade diz sobre o grupo (sem ecoar meros rumores); compreender que a “intelligence” (informação) não se resume à espionagem — é também a perceção de padrões sociais repetidos; evitar confundir o relato das fontes com a verdade absoluta — toda a informação deve ser verificada, cruzada e ponderada. Referências externas para aprofundamento (Nível 3) UNODC — Gabinete das Nações Unidas contra a Droga e o Crime — materiais sobre estruturas criminosas transnacionais e respostas do Estado. INTERPOL — Recursos sobre criminalidade organizada e cooperação internacional . ICAO — Normas e padrões de cooperação em investigações internacionais (contexto de apoio técnico). Materiais de análise de redes (teoria de grafos aplicada à análise de relações) e de inteligência de fontes abertas (OSINT) — consulte orientações nacionais e internacionais sobre o uso ético. Agora que leu os três níveis, veja um exemplo concreto de como as abordagens diferem. Ir ao Exemplo Real Exemplo Real Polícia e Militares: como as abordagens diferem entre países — e porque razão a distinção recai sempre sobre o crime e a inocência Não existe uma “polícia portuguesa vs. militar francesa vs. polícia italiana” como modelos mutuamente exclusivos. Existe uma variedade de modelos nacionais , cada um com os seus limites, formas e normas. Contudo, o princípio é transversal: o crime é crime, o inocente é inocente — onde quer que ocorram. 4.1 Tipos de modelos de forças de segurança (visão panorâmica) Polícia civil unificada — modelo em que a polícia constitui a principal força de segurança no domínio civil, com funções de investigação, prevenção e resposta, podendo contemplar detalhes por tipo de crime (por exemplo, polícia judiciária, forças especiais). Forças armadas com papel interno — em determinados países, as forças armadas podem desempenhar um papel na segurança interna em situações específicas (estado de sítio, operações de apoio, segurança de infraestruturas críticas). A presença militar interna deve ser excecional e estritamente regulada. Modelos com forças especializadas — alguns países organizam forças consoante o tipo de ameaça (unidades de resposta rápida, unidades de investigação criminal, unidades de inteligência). A especialização tem valor quando existem competências distintas, mas não deve substituir a coordenação legal. Coordenação internacional — muitas ameaças são transnacionais, pelo que a resposta ocorre frequentemente através de cooperação (INTERPOL, Europol, acordos bilaterais, partilha de inteligência). 4.2 O que muda entre países (e o que permanece igual) Dimensão O que varia O que não varia Enquadramento legal de cada força Estatutos, competências, limites de uso da força, procedimentos de detenção. Nenhuma força de Estado pode ignorar o princípio de que atos criminosos cometidos por agentes constituem crimes. Relação entre militares e civis Cada país define quando e de que forma as forças armadas podem intervir internamente. A distinção entre inocente e criminoso não desaparece pela presença de tropas nas ruas. Estrutura de investigação Nível de especialização, coordenação entre serviços, papel da inteligência. A prova e o devido processo legal são obrigatórios em qualquer sistema que pretenda ser justo. Cooperação internacional Grau de integração em redes regionais e globais. A criminalidade organizada não respeita fronteiras — a resposta não pode cingir-se ao plano puramente nacional. 4.3 A diferença real entre polícias — um exemplo concreto Consideremos uma situação hipotética (mas estruturalmente comum): uma organização criminosa que opera através de redes de comércio fictícias , com comunicação encriptada e presença em múltiplas jurisdições. Abordagem puramente repressiva (modelo rígido) : operação simultânea em múltiplos pontos, detenções genéricas, apreensões massivas. Vantagem: impacto rápido. Risco: detenção de pessoas sem ligação relevante; provas frágeis; desconfiança da comunidade; reação de adaptação rápida por parte do grupo. Abordagem de inteligência e análise (modelo de leitura) : mapeamento da estrutura, identificação de centros e pontes, distinção entre elementos centrais e periféricos, atuação sobre indicadores específicos. Vantagem: precisão, menor risco de erro face a inocentes, preservação da legitimidade. Requer tempo, coordenação e rigor. Ambas podem ser necessárias em momentos distintos. O erro ocorre quando se utiliza apenas uma por impulso, ou quando a via repressiva é usada para substituir a análise. 4.4 A mesma falha em qualquer contexto Se uma polícia portuguesa comete um excesso, constitui um erro português. Se uma força militar italiana excede a autorização interna, constitui um erro italiano. Se uma polícia francesa desrespeita um inocente, constitui um erro francês. Se um elemento policial ou militar de qualquer país comete um crime, o crime é crime . Um ato criminoso não se torna “menos crime” por ser praticado por um Estado ou instituição. Princípio O Estado que atua com as mãos sujas perde a autoridade moral para agir — mesmo que o outro lado seja criminoso. Por seu turno, o criminoso não se torna “menos criminoso” pelo facto de a polícia ter agido incorretamente. Dois erros não melhoram o mundo; tornam ambos os lados ilegítimos. 4.5 Resposta correta: precisão e não exagero coordenar a atuação entre jurisdições quando a rede é transnacional; distinguir os membros efetivos da estrutura criminosa daqueles que são periféricos, inocentes ou meramente relacionados por proximidade; agir com base em provas, e não em pressões mediáticas ou reputacionais; manter a transparência interna e externa no tocante às decisões — porque demonstrar que a força atua dentro de limites é o que garante a sua legitimidade. C) Quem nunca se desloca é considerado inocente. 2. Um investigador pensa: “A organização criminosa já foi violenta, logo a polícia também pode exagerar.” Esta constitui uma boa decisão? A) Sim, porque o crime justifica o crime. B) Não, trata-se de uma dupla medida — substitui a lei pela retaliação e compromete a legitimidade do Estado. C) Depende do país em questão. 3. Na leitura de redes criminosas, quem é frequentemente o verdadeiro centro de comando? A) Quem aparece mais vezes na comunicação pública. B) A pessoa que corrige o rumo quando a operação falha, mesmo que não seja a mais visível. C) Quem nunca aparece. 4. Relativamente a uma rede criminosa, é sempre necessário efetuar detenções ou usar a força pelo simples facto de a rede existir? A) Sim, porque a existência da rede constitui prova de crime contra todos os membros. B) Não — muitas vezes o problema afeta apenas uma parte da rede; a decisão deve ser precisa, proporcional e fundamentada em provas. C) Apenas se houver pressão política. 5. Um crime cometido por um agente de polícia ou militar constitui: A) Um ato menos grave, pois o agente atua no interesse do Estado. B) Um crime — idêntico na sua natureza a qualquer outro; a origem institucional não diminui a ilegalidade. C) Uma conduta aceitável se o grupo-alvo também for criminoso. 6. C) Não é possível obter qualquer conhecimento sem pertencer ao grupo. 7. B) A legislação define competências e limites, mas o princípio de que o crime é crime e o inocente é inocente não varia com a nacionalidade. C) Não existem diferenças — todos os países aplicam exatamente os mesmos métodos. Nentoo: What "we" Know Gentoo Linux is a Source Based distribution that ask users to compile all software. While it gives a sensation of control, software compatibility is very restricted and their repositories have a lot of software that is out of date and incompatible to install on Gentoo, without facing more problems on compilation time. The Unique aspect of control that can give, it to those users who know the work of LFS aka Linux From Scratch , and want that process automated, while LFS don't face so much problems installing software. After that, Gentoo offer the possibility to manage compatibility in Software, using the USE flags, that are "words" defined on the software, pointing into the compatibility. For example, Vim on Gentoo , can be installed without the Graphical interface, by adding something like this: app-editors/vim -X . With that value placed in the correct path /etc/portage/package.use/ , as a content of the filename of the software(vim), Gentoo knows that Vim , will not have Graphical compatibility. It simplifies the process of installing software without personalizing it with the core options that the authors give. In fact, all that painful process of extracting to / or other path each library and applications, ./configure --help Options, that can be More deeper than what Gentoo gives to users, and the make & make install to install software, can have extra options too. Since Gentoo wish to simplify that process, Gentoo serve that purpose only . A interesting aspect between Gentoo and FreeBSD , is that Gentoo change the magic words of software compatibility when compiling, while FreeBSD don't care what "software compatibility" you want, when compiling software from ports . The "reconfig" option when compiling software using FreeBSD ports, is the best option to save you time. Else, you will need to Monitor compilation process, waiting for a new "popup" about software compatibility, of each extra software that some software ask as dependency. In the other hand/side, Debian already compile everything and offer the same, almost all other Linux Distros offer: Binary Packages (already compiled software). What can take days (in case of using Linux From Scratch ) or some hours (in case of using Gentoo ) all other distros save that time for you, while software compatibility make use of all options available on each software.

Click any wall to open its internals, code and sources. 🛡 pledge(2) — voluntary amputation of power + What: a process declares which syscall groups it needs — e.g. stdio rpath wpath cpath inet dns — and the kernel kills it ( SIGABRT ) if it ever touches anything else. Promises can only shrink, never grow. A compromised httpd parser that pledged stdio rpath cannot exec , open sockets, or ptrace — the exploit dies inside the sandbox it built itself. copy /* httpd render path: after parsing config, drop everything */ #include <unistd.h> if (pledge( "stdio rpath" , NULL) == -1) err(1, "pledge" ); /* from here: no exec, no socket, no prot_exec — RCE becomes DoS */ Why secure: moves policy into the program where intent is known; tiny API (one call) so adoption is massive — 500+ base programs pledged. Combines with unveil for least privilege in two dimensions. Sources: pledge(2) manual · innovations · sshd + privsep 👁 unveil(2) — the filesystem you can't see doesn't exist + What: grant visibility to only chosen paths with chosen rights ( rwxc ), then lock: unveil("/var/www","r"); unveil(NULL,NULL) . Everything else returns ENOENT — directory traversal, /etc/passwd reads, key theft all fail closed. Perfect pair: pledge limits what calls , unveil limits what files . copy /* static file server: see only /var/www, read-only */ unveil( "/var/www" , "r" ); unveil( "/var/www/logs" , "rwc" ); if (pledge( "stdio rpath wpath cpath" , NULL) == -1) err(1, "pledge" ); unveil(NULL, NULL); // lock: no more unveil calls Sources: unveil(2) · innovations ✖ W^X — memory is writable XOR executable, never both + What: since 3.3, strict by default in 6.0: no page may be WRITE+EXEC . Reality is duller and far more effective: an unlocked door, a stolen password, an unpatched server nobody remembered was facing the internet. This guide walks the eight levels of real intrusion technique, with a documented case file, a code sample and the defense that would have stopped it at each one. 8 levels of technique Documented case files Mapped to MITRE ATT&CK Every claim sourced ~60% of breaches involved a human element (Verizon DBIR 2025) 44% of breaches involved ransomware, up 37% year over year (DBIR 2025) 30% of breaches involved a third party — double the prior year (DBIR 2025) 20% used exploitation of a vulnerability to get in, +34% YoY (DBIR 2025) $115k median ransom actually paid; 64% of victims refused to pay (DBIR 2025) Reality vs. the movies Start here Real intrusions are not spells. They are a sequence of unremarkable steps, each one cheap, each one avoidable. The industry has a shared vocabulary for those steps — MITRE ATT&CK, which currently catalogues 15 tactics, 227 techniques and 479 sub-techniques for enterprise environments alone [1] [2] . This page follows that shape, level by level. Myth: hackers break cryptography Modern encryption is not the weak point. They log in with someone's valid password instead. Reality Valid accounts and stolen credentials recur in nearly every case below. In the 2024 Snowflake intrusions, every incident investigated traced back to compromised customer credentials [37] . Myth: it takes a genius Attack tooling is commoditised, sold as a subscription, and often operated by people who understand the business poorly and the tooling not at all. Reality The MGM Resorts intrusion was not won with an exploit. It was won by persuading a help desk to reset a password [19] . The victim's filing put the impact at roughly $100 million [18] . Myth: zero-days are required Zero-days are expensive, perishable ammunition. Most intrusions use a vulnerability the vendor patched months ago — or no vulnerability at all. Reality Change Healthcare in 2024 was not a novel attack: a system simply wasn't using multifactor authentication [20] . Myth: it's over in seconds Dwell time is long. SUNBURST, the SolarWinds backdoor, deliberately waited roughly two weeks before even phoning home. Reality Detection rarely fails because the attacker was fast. It fails because nobody was looking at the logs that already said what happened. The ladder, at a glance Levels 0–4 are about getting in . Levels 5–6 are about staying in and getting around . Levels 7–8 are about what the access is worth . An attacker rarely needs all eight — most intrusions end at level 2 or 3 and still work. Level What it really means ATT&CK anchor Cost to attacker 0 · Recon Read what the target published: services, staff, secrets, software versions TA0043 Near zero 1 · Default creds Log in to a device still using the factory password T1078, T1110 Near zero 2 · Reuse Try passwords stolen from other breaches against this one T1110.004 Very low 3 · Social engineering Persuade a person to hand over access or approve a prompt T1566, T1078 Low, scales 4 · Exploit a service Abuse a software flaw in something reachable from the internet T1190 Low to high 5 · Escalate & move Turn one foothold into domain-wide control, quietly T1003, T1550.002 Moderate 6 · Persist & exfiltrate Beacon home on a schedule, blend with normal traffic, take the data T1071, T1219 Moderate 7 · Impact Encrypt, leak, sell, extort or commit fraud TA0040 Low once inside 8 · Nation-state Supply-chain code, purpose-built zero-days, air-gap crossing T1195, T1190 Very high Read the ladder as a budget. Every rung is a trade: sophistication costs money and risks attention; an unlocked door costs nothing and often works. That is why the boring rungs — 1, 2 and 3 — carry most of the real intrusions, and why the exotic rung 8 gets the headlines. Level 0 · Reconnaissance 0 Seeing what you left facing the internet MITRE ATT&CK TA0043 Reconnaissance · “Hacking” begins with reading, not breaking. Before anything is attacked, it is measured. Public-facing IP ranges are scanned continuously and indexed: which hosts, which ports, which software versions. Subdomains leak in certificate transparency logs. Job adverts name the exact products a company runs. Source-code repositories leak far more than code — sometimes live credentials. None of this is illegal in most jurisdictions, and all of it is automated. The attacker's real question at this level is simple: what is exposed, and who can log into it? Case file Uber, 2016 — the key that was sitting in Git The access chain behind Uber's 2016 breach is a perfect illustration of levels 0, 2 and 3 stacked together. According to the US Federal Trade Commission, an engineer had placed an AWS access key in plain text inside a private GitHub repository , and the intruders reached those repositories using engineer passwords exposed in other large data breaches — Uber did not require MFA for repository access and did not prohibit password reuse [25] . The FTC's figures: over one month, intruders downloaded 25.6 million names and email addresses , 22.1 million names and mobile numbers , and 607,000 driver's-licence numbers [25] . California's Attorney General described the exposure as data of 57 million users ; Uber later settled nationwide for $148 million over the breach and the delayed disclosure [26] . Two mundane controls — mandatory MFA on the code host, and never storing long-lived keys in a repository — would each have broken the chain. secret-hunt — what a repo leak looks like from outside bash # One command over a repo's entire history, including deleted files. # (These two values are AWS's own public documentation examples.) $ git log -p --all | grep -nE 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}' +aws_access_key_id = AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE +aws_secret_access_key = wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY # Deleted commits are not deleted. History is the leak surface. $ git log --all --oneline -- .env 4f9a1c2 rotate keys a03bb77 initial commit <-- the secret still lives here the fix — remove the long-lived key entirely ini # ~/.aws/config — no stored secret to steal in the first place. [default] region = us-east-1 credential_process = aws-sso-credential-process # Or, in CI, an OIDC workload identity that mints short-lived # credentials per job. Nothing long-lived to leak, nothing to rotate. Why “private repository” is not a security control A private repo is an authorisation decision made by one vendor, protecting a secret you do not control, sitting behind a password that a human chose and may reuse. It is one factor. Once an attacker holds a valid engineer session — as in the Uber case — private and public look identical. Treat every repository as eventually public and every key as eventually leaked: that is why short-lived, scoped credentials beat long-lived ones regardless of where they live. What stops it Secret scanning in the pipeline , plus history scanning — catch the key before a human forgets it. No long-lived cloud keys. Use SSO, OIDC and workload identity so there is nothing durable to steal. Cut your internet surface. Inventory what is actually reachable; kill forgotten endpoints and test environments. Mandatory MFA on the code host — this alone broke the Uber chain at the first step. Level 1 · The unlocked front door 1 Devices still using the factory password MITRE ATT&CK T1078 Valid Accounts · T1110 Brute Force · Default and weak credentials The cheapest possible intrusion: a device that ships with admin/admin , is never changed, and is reachable from the internet on an administrative port. No exploit, no cleverness — just a login form left as the vendor designed it. Case file Mirai, 2016 — 62 default passwords, one botnet Mirai scanned the internet continuously for internet-of-things devices — routers, cameras, DVRs — and logged in with a list of 62 common default usernames and passwords . Each compromised device joined a botnet used for distributed denial-of-service attacks. CISA advised network defenders to watch Telnet ports 23 and 2323 for unauthorised access attempts [29] . CISA attributed a DDoS exceeding 620 Gbps against KrebsOnSecurity to Mirai, and a separate Mirai attack on OVH of at least 1.1 Tbps [29] . CISA cited the Mirai author's claim of more than 380,000 IoT devices enlisted for the Krebs attack [29] . Mirai was also associated with the October 2016 Dyn DNS outage, which made major sites briefly unreachable for many users; the SEI's write-up describes Mirai's role cautiously, as one factor among several [30] . No CVE was needed for the original mechanism. The weakness was a known default credential on an exposed port. /var/log/auth.log — the shape of the attack, from the defender's side text $ grep -E 'Failed password|Invalid user' /var/log/auth.log | tail -6 Oct 16 03:14:02 host sshd[2919]: Invalid user admin from 185.203.16.77 port 51422 Oct 16 03:14:03 host sshd[2921]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 185.203.16.77 port 51438 Oct 16 03:14:04 host sshd[2923]: Invalid user root from 185.203.16.77 port 51451 Oct 16 03:14:05 host sshd[2925]: Failed password for invalid user root from 185.203.16.77 port 51466 Oct 16 03:14:06 host sshd[2927]: Invalid user pi from 185.203.16.77 port 51479 Oct 16 03:14:07 host sshd[2929]: Failed password for invalid user pi from 185.203.16.77 port 51491 # Rank sources by failed-auth volume. (Field position varies with the # message shape, so pin it with a named-pattern parser in production.) $ grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log \ | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3 4182 185.203.16.77 <-- block this source and investigate 91 91.240.118.4 12 172.16.4.19 <-- internal, wrong password: talk to that user the fix — make the default impossible and unreachable jsonc // The remedy is deliberately boring, which is why it gets skipped. { "device" : "camera-fw-4.2" , "change_on_first_boot" : [ "admin" ], // enforced at setup, not suggested "telnet" : { "enabled" : false }, // the port Mirai needed "mgmt_interface" : "vlan-99" , // reachable from the mgmt network only "egress_policy" : "deny-by-default" // a compromised camera cannot call out } What stops it Change defaults at onboarding , on a process that fails closed if the step is skipped. Turn off what you don't use: Telnet, UPnP, vendor cloud bridges, debug ports. Segment the device class. Cameras and printers should not reach the finance VLAN or the internet freely. Rate-limit and alert on authentication failures per source, and block or tarpit on threshold. Inventory the unowned. Most default-credential casualties are devices no one knows they own. Level 2 · Password reuse & credential stuffing 2 Your password was valid here because it was valid somewhere else MITRE ATT&CK T1110.004 Credential Stuffing · T1078 Valid Accounts · T1555 Credentials from Password Stores Credential stuffing takes username/password pairs leaked from one service and tries them on another, exploiting the fact that people reuse passwords. MITRE describes the technique as gaining access through “ credential overlap ” — users reusing passwords across personal and business accounts [36] . Add infostealer malware, which harvests saved credentials and session data from a victim's own machine and uploads them to a marketplace, and the attacker never needs to break anything at all. They are simply logging in as an employee. Case file The 2024 Snowflake campaign — AT&T, Ticketmaster, Santander This is the reference example of level 2 at scale. Mandiant tracked the financially motivated actor as UNC5537 and reported that every incident it investigated was traced back to compromised customer credentials , with no evidence the activity came from a breach of Snowflake's own environment. The credentials had previously been stolen by infostealer malware on systems that were not Snowflake's; at least 79.7% of the accounts the actor used had prior credential exposure. In the incidents analysed, MFA was not enabled, valid credentials had sometimes gone unrotated for years, and network allow lists were absent. Mandiant and Snowflake had notified approximately 165 potentially exposed organisations [37] . AT&T told the SEC that an attacker accessed a workspace on a third-party cloud platform and exfiltrated files between April 14 and April 25, 2024 . The data covered call and text-interaction records for roughly May–October 2022 and one day in January 2023, and the filing says it covered “nearly all of AT&T's wireless customers.” The filing itself does not state a numeric total [38] . The widely reported figure of roughly 109 million US customer accounts comes from contemporaneous reporting and describes accounts, not individual call records [39] [40] . Ticketmaster confirmed “unauthorized activity on an isolated cloud database hosted by a third-party data services provider” and did not name the provider or confirm the frequently repeated 560-million figure [41] . Santander confirmed unauthorised access to a third-party-hosted database affecting certain customers in Chile, Spain and Uruguay, while stating that no credentials allowing transactions were contained in that database [42] . Case file 23andMe, 2023 — 14,000 logins, 6.9 million profiles A useful lesson in reading breach numbers carefully. 23andMe said an actor accessed a select number of individual accounts using credential stuffing — credentials reused from other compromised websites . The confirmed figure was roughly 14,000 accounts , under 0.1% of its customers. Through those accounts, the actor reached approximately 5.5 million DNA Relatives profiles and 1.4 million Family Tree profiles — about 6.9 million profiles in total , which is not the same as 6.9 million compromised logins [43] . Fourteen thousand reused passwords produced a headline about nearly seven million people: the blast radius of one login is every other account it can see . Vendor measurement of the underlying behaviour: SpyCloud reported a 74% reuse rate among users exposed in two or more breaches during the prior year, and a 61% historical reuse rate for previously exposed passwords through 2023. These describe SpyCloud's analysed exposure population, not a survey of all internet users [44] [45] . login.py — the version that feeds credential stuffing python # ✖ Fast hash, no rate limit, verbose errors, no MFA gate. import hashlib def login (db, email, password): row = db.execute( "SELECT pw_hash FROM users WHERE email = ?" , (email,) ).fetchone() if row is None : return "No account with that email" # enumeration: tells the attacker who exists if row[ "pw_hash" ] == hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest(): return "ok" # MD5: billions of guesses per second on a GPU return "Wrong password" # and nothing limits how often this runs login.py — hardened for exactly this attack python # ✓ Memory-hard hash, per-source throttle, uniform responses, MFA continuation. from argon2 import PasswordHasher from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError ph = PasswordHasher() def login (db, cache, email, password, ip, device): # 1. WHERE id = ?" , (ph.hash(password), row[ "id" ])) return require_mfa (row[ "id" ], device) # password alone is not a session except VerifyMismatchError: pass return generic_failure () # no enumeration, no detail, no oracle The MFA line is the whole defense. In the Snowflake campaign, credentials were valid but MFA was simply not enabled, and in some cases the same credential had gone unrotated for years [37] . A stolen password plus a second factor the attacker does not have is just a failed login. What stops it MFA everywhere, then make it phishing-resistant (see level 3) — this defeats stolen passwords outright. Argon2id or bcrypt for storage, so a stolen hash is not a cheap offline crack. Screen passwords against breach corpora at set-password and login time — a reused password is a known password. Throttle per account and per IP , with uniform error messages to avoid account enumeration. Rotate and scope service credentials , and set network allow lists where the vendor supports them. Assume endpoint compromise. Infostealers make credential theft trivial; endpoint hardening is a credential control too. Level 3 · Social engineering 3 Hacking the people who legitimately have access MITRE ATT&CK T1566 Phishing · T1078 Valid Accounts · MFA fatigue / help-desk impersonation Social engineering is not a lesser form of hacking; it is the highest-yield one, because it targets the component that is hardest to patch and most willing to be helpful. Three variants dominate real incidents: Phishing — a message that convinces a person to enter credentials on a page the attacker controls, or to open an attachment. MFA fatigue / push bombing — the attacker already holds the password and repeatedly triggers push prompts until the victim approves one out of irritation or confusion. Help-desk impersonation — the attacker calls the service desk as an employee, and asks them to reset the password or enrol a new authenticator. Case file MGM Resorts, 2023 — a help desk, not an exploit Public reporting attributes the intrusion to the Scattered Spider group using help-desk social engineering. CISA's advisory on the group describes precisely this tactic: persuading help-desk staff to reset passwords or reissue MFA tokens. MGM's own SEC filing does not state the initial-access method or name the actors, so the specific reported impersonation sequence is press attribution rather than a company confirmation [18] [19] . MGM estimated a negative impact of approximately $100 million to Adjusted Property EBITDAR and reported less than $10 million in one-time expenses at that point [18] . The filing says personal information was obtained for some customers who had transacted before March 2019 , and that bank-account and payment-card information were not obtained [18] . No CVE. Nothing was exploited — the account-recovery process was. Case file Target, 2013 — a contractor's credentials, and 40 million cards Attackers entered Target's network using network credentials stolen from Fazio Mechanical Services , Target's HVAC and refrigeration contractor. They then placed card-stealing malware on point-of-sale systems and moved the stolen data out to external drop servers. Reporting attributes the credential theft to a malware-bearing phishing email; the readable account confirms the stolen vendor credentials as the entry, and establishes phishing less firmly [21] [22] . Approximately 40 million debit and credit card accounts were exposed [21] . Target's 2015 filing is reported to show $252 million in cumulative breach expenses, offset by $90 million of insurance, for a net $162 million [23] . The control failure was not a missing patch. V Vim Master Guide Pure Vanilla Text Architecture v9.0 / Neovim Zero to Hero Mastery Master Text Editing at the Speed of Thought Vim isn't just a text editor—it is a composable, domain-specific language for manipulating text. Stop using arrows and mouse clicks; start speaking Vim. The Grammar: [Count] + [Operator / Verb] + [Text Object / Motion] 01. Introduction & Modal Philosophy Traditional editors assume every key press inserts text. Vim assumes you spend most of your time reading, navigating, and refactoring code, reserving typing for specific modes. Normal Mode Esc / Ctrl+[ The command hub. Keys act as actions, navigation commands, and operators rather than text inputs. Insert Mode i / a / o Standard typing mode. Keypresses insert literal characters into the active buffer. Visual Mode v / V / Ctrl+v Highlight text regions character-wise ( v ), line-wise ( V ), or block-wise ( Ctrl+v ). Command-Line : / ? / ! Execute Ex commands for saving, quitting, buffer operations, search, and system execution. Select Mode gh Behaves like traditional IDE text highlighting where typing immediately overwrites selection. Terminal Mode :terminal Interacts with an embedded terminal shell directly inside a Vim window split. 02. Basic Navigation & Fundamental Editing Master home-row navigation and fundamental editing mechanics before learning complex sequences. Category Keys Action Description Core Directional h j k l Left, Down, Up, Right (keep hands on home-row) Word Motions w / W | b / B Next word / WORD start | Previous word / WORD start Word Endings e / E | ge / gE Forward to end of word / WORD | Backward to end of word / WORD Line Bounds 0 | ^ | $ Column 0 (absolute start) | First non-whitespace char | End of line Inline Character Find f{char} / t{char} Find character forward / Till character forward (place cursor before) Repeat Find ; / , Repeat last f/t search forward / Repeat backward Vertical Paging Ctrl+u / Ctrl+d Scroll half-page Up / Scroll half-page Down File Navigation gg / G | {num}G First line of buffer / Last line of buffer | Jump directly to line {num} The Dot Operator (.) The single most powerful core command in Vim. . repeats the last editing change (e.g., cw + type word + Esc , then hit . on another word to instantly replace it). 03. Text Objects & Advanced Motions Text objects allow operating on structural constructs (words, quotes, brackets, tags) regardless of where the cursor is inside the object. Inner ( i ) vs Around ( a ) i targets only the content inside the boundaries. a targets the content PLUS surrounding delimiters & whitespace . Common Target Objects w / s / p - Words, Sentences, Paragraphs " , ' , ` - Single, Double, or Backtick Quotes ( , [ , { , < - Parentheses, Brackets, Braces, Angle brackets t - HTML / XML Tags Expression Command Target Text Resulting Action ciw const variable = true; Deletes inner word and drops into Insert mode. di" console.log(" Hello World "); Wipes text inside quotes, keeping empty quotes "" . da( func (arg1, arg2) ; Deletes parentheses AND everything contained inside. cit

Page Title

Changes contents between opening and closing HTML tags. 04. Registers, Marks & Macros Store text snippets, bookmark arbitrary code lines, and record repetitive keystroke sequences for massive automation. Key Registers "{reg} "" Unnamed register (last delete/yank) "0 Last yank register (unaffected by deletes) "+ System Clipboard (OS copy/paste) "_ Blackhole register (discards text) "= Expression evaluation calculator Jump Marks m{mark} ma Set local mark a for current buffer mA Set global mark A across buffers 'a Jump to line of mark a `a Jump to exact column & line of mark a '' Jump back to location before last jump Macros q{reg} qa Start recording keystrokes into register a q Stop recording macro @a Execute macro a once @@ Repeat last executed macro 10@a Run macro a 10 times consecutively 05. Splits, Buffers, Windows & Tabs Understand the core distinction: A Buffer is a file loaded into memory. A Window is a viewport into a buffer. A Tab is a collection of window viewports. Buffer Operations :ls or :buffers — List active memory buffers :bnext ( :bn ) / :bprev ( :bp ) — Cycle buffers :b {num_or_name} — Switch to buffer ID or partial match :bdelete ( :bd ) — Unload buffer without quitting Window Splits :sp / :vsp — Horizontal / Vertical window split Ctrl+w h/j/k/l — Move focus between split directions Ctrl+w = — Equalize dimensions of all open splits Ctrl+w o — Close all splits except current active window 06. Power User Built-in Features (Zero Plugins Required) Vim comes out of the box with built-in tools that eliminate the absolute necessity for third-party extensions. Built-In Power Workflows " 1. Netrw File Explorer (Native file tree) :Ex " Open Netrw file explorer in current window :Vex " Open Netrw in vertical split " Inside Netrw: 'd' creates dir, '%' creates file, 'R' renames " 2. Global Command (:g) - Run Ex actions on pattern matches :g /^$/ d " Delete all empty lines in entire file :g /TODO/ t$ " Copy all lines containing 'TODO' to end of file :v /DEBUG/ d " Delete all lines that DO NOT match 'DEBUG' " 3. Quickfix List - Project-wide Search & Replace :vimgrep /getUser/ src/**/*.ts :copen " Open quickfix results window :cfdo %s/getUser/fetchUser/g | update " Batch substitute across all search files " 4. Native Autocompletion (Insert Mode) Ctrl+n / Ctrl+p " Keyword match in current / open buffers Ctrl+x Ctrl+f " File path autocompletion Ctrl+x Ctrl+l " Whole line autocompletion 07. The Ultimate Vanilla .vimrc Masterclass A production-ready, sensible configuration file written in standard Vimscript. ~/.vimrc " ============================================================================ " PRODUCTION-READY VANILLA .VIMRC " ============================================================================ set nocompatible " Disable Vi compatibility mode filetype plugin indent on " Enable filetype detection and auto-indent syntax on " Enable syntax highlighting " --- UI Settings --- set number " Absolute line number on cursor set relativenumber " Relative line numbers for easy jump motions set cursorline " Highlight current line set scrolloff= 8 " Keep 8 padding lines visible above/below cursor set signcolumn=yes " Always display sign column to prevent layout shifts set termguicolors " Enable 24-bit True Color support set wildmenu " Enhanced visual command-line completion set wildmode=longest:full,full " --- Indentation & Tabs --- set tabstop= 4 " Visual spaces per TAB set softtabstop= 4 " Spaces inserted while editing set shiftwidth= 4 " Spaces used for auto-indenting set expandtab " Convert tabs to spaces set autoindent smartindent " Smart code indentation logic " --- Search & Splitting --- set ignorecase smartcase " Case-insensitive unless query contains Capital set incsearch hlsearch " Incremental search & persistent highlights set splitbelow splitright " Natural split orientation (bottom & right) " --- History & Undo --- set hidden " Allow switching buffers without saving set undofile " Persistent undo trees saved across reboots set undodir=~/.vim/undodir " --- Custom Keymappings --- let mapleader = " " " Set Spacebar as Leader key " Fast saving & quitting nnoremap w :w nnoremap q :q " Clear search highlight using Space + h nnoremap h :nohlsearch " Keep selection highlighted when shifting indents vnoremap < >gv 08. Telescope.nvim / fzf.vim Fuzzy Finder Asynchronous fuzzy search windows over files, git commits, LSP symbols, and live project grep results. nvim-treesitter Syntax Parsing Uses incremental AST parsers for context-aware syntax highlighting, scope selection, and code folding. Mason & nvim-lspconfig LSP Integration Seamlessly installs and hooks language servers directly into built-in autocompletion and linting diagnostics.
